**The Tuner**

The house was the kind that had once been proud and had since settled into being merely large. Marek parked on the gravel and sat for a moment with the engine off, listening to the ticking of it cooling. He had learned over thirty years that the first minute told you most of what you needed to know. Whether the family kept the piano in a sunroom, where the heat would have warped it slowly for a decade. Whether children lived there. Whether anyone had opened the lid since the last time someone died.

The woman who answered the door was in her sixties and wore a cardigan with a stain near the pocket that she hadn't noticed or had stopped caring about. She said her name was Ilse. She said the piano had been her mother's.

"When was it last tuned?"

She thought about it the way people think about questions they know the answer to but don't want to say. "Nineteen ninety-something."

"That's all right," he said, and meant it. Neglect was honest. It was the pianos that had been tuned every six months by someone careless that broke his heart.

The instrument was in the front room, under a window with heavy curtains half-drawn. A Bösendorfer, which surprised him. Not the kind of thing you expected in a house like this, in a town like this. Somebody had loved it very much once, or had wanted very much to be the kind of person who owned one. Both, probably. Those were rarely different things.

He lifted the lid and the smell came up—felt and old wood and the faint metallic sweetness of strings that have been sitting still for a long time. Dust lay along the soundboard in a soft grey sheet. He didn't brush it away yet. He struck middle C.

It was a quarter tone flat, more or less, and the unison was so far spread that the note wobbled like a voice about to cry. But underneath the wobble the tone itself was still there—round, dark, a little melancholy even when it wasn't trying to be. He played a few more notes up the register and felt the familiar small relief. The frame was sound. The board hadn't cracked. Everything wrong with it was something he could fix.

"Is it bad?" Ilse asked from the doorway.

"It's just been waiting," he said.

He worked for two hours. She brought him coffee at one point and set it down without speaking, then stood a while by the bookshelf pretending to look at the spines. He was used to this. People couldn't help hovering when you touched a thing that belonged to their dead. He set his mutes, laid the hammer on the pin, and pulled the string up toward where it belonged, listening for the beats to slow and vanish. There is a particular moment in tuning a unison when two strings that have been arguing for years stop arguing. The sound doesn't get louder. It gets *still*. Every time, some small animal part of him relaxed at that stillness, as if it were his own quarrel that had ended.

Around the third octave she spoke.

"She played every evening. Even at the end, when she couldn't remember much else. She'd forget my name and then sit down and play the whole of the Schubert B-flat without a mistake."

Marek nodded and kept working. He'd heard this story, or its cousins, perhaps a hundred times. It never became less true.

"After she died I couldn't stand to hear it. And then I couldn't stand to sell it. So." She gestured at the years.

"That's usually how it goes."

"Do you play?"

"Badly. Enough to check my work." He set another mute. "I was going to be a pianist. Then I found out I was better at listening than at making anyone else listen."

She smiled at that, the first time. He liked her for it.

When he finished he played a slow C major chord, then an arpeggio up through four octaves, then a few bars of something—he didn't decide what, his hands decided—that turned out to be the opening of the Schubert. He hadn't meant it as a gesture. He stopped after eight bars because he knew he'd start making mistakes and didn't want to spoil it.

The room had changed. It was the same room, the same curtains and dust, but sound had entered it properly again, had gone into the corners and touched the walls and come back. He had done this thousands of times and still didn't understand it fully, how an instrument brought back into tune seemed to tune the space around it. As if the house had been holding its breath.

Ilse was crying a little, in the undemonstrative way of people who cried often and privately and had stopped apologizing for it.

"It sounds like her," she said.

"It sounds like itself," he said, gently. "It always did. She just knew how to let it."

He packed his tools. At the door she paid him in cash from an envelope that had clearly been set aside for this, counted in advance, the way his own mother had once counted out money for things that mattered. She asked when he should come back.

"Six months. Then a year. It'll hold better now that it's been woken up."

Driving home he thought, as he often did, that his trade was mostly a matter of undoing time. Not reversing it—nothing did that—but relieving things of its weight. Strings stretched, wood swelled and shrank, everything drifted from where it was meant to be. You couldn't stop the drifting. You could only come around every so often and, with patience and a hammer and a good ear, remind a thing what it had sounded like when someone first loved it.

The car ticked. The road ran flat between fields. Somewhere behind him, in the front room of a house that had settled into being merely large, a woman was sitting down at a piano for the first time in a long while, lifting the lid, and beginning—slowly, and not without mistakes—to play.
